name: Access to Grade Level Content
title: Access to Grade Level Content
answer: Access to grade level content means giving English learners versions of the same material that keep the key ideas and vocabulary but simplify the language, so they can learn the subject rather than being shut out by reading difficulty. It matters because a student who cannot read the science textbook cannot learn the science, and because the research the book cites shows technology built into planned instruction works far better than technology added on the side.

sections.body: The idea starts from a simple problem: English learners are often expected to learn grade level content from texts they cannot yet read. Teachers can use tools such as MagicSchool or Newsela to produce versions of a text at different language levels, holding on to the key ideas and vocabulary while making sentence structure simpler. The teacher then checks that the simpler version still teaches the same content. Alongside leveled texts, the book describes unit glossaries of key terms with simple definitions, examples and home language translations, and sentence frames that give students the structures to talk and write about content before they can build those sentences alone. Together these moves solve the access problem without lowering the content.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: In a classroom, a teacher takes a text the class is studying and produces leveled versions for students at different language levels, then confirms the simpler version still carries the same content. The leveled text is used inside a planned lesson rather than handed out on its own. For vocabulary, the teacher uses AI to draft a unit glossary of key terms with simple definitions, examples and translations into students' home languages through Microsoft Translator, and a bilingual staff member reviews the translations because academic terms are often translated poorly. The glossary then serves as a reference students return to throughout the unit. For speaking and writing, the teacher uses MagicSchool to generate sentence frames at several proficiency levels, with early level students using simpler frames such as "I think the answer is _ because _" and more advanced students using frames that push toward academic language.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The book labels this idea with research support. It cites a meta analysis of 42 samples of English learners which found that literacy instruction with technology built in had a medium sized effect over instruction without it (Lee, 2020). It also cites a meta analysis of studies in China which found that comprehensive programs with technology at their core had much larger effects than supplementary activities added on the side, which had almost none (Ni et al., 2022). The book draws the practical conclusion from these findings that a leveled text works best when it is part of a planned lesson, not a handout.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The teacher stays responsible for checking that a simplified version still teaches the same content, so leveling does not quietly become a reduction in what is taught. Translations drafted with AI must be reviewed by a bilingual staff member, because academic terms are often translated poorly. The book also sets a limit on how technology is used: programs with technology at their core outperform activities added on the side, so a leveled text or a generated frame should sit inside planned instruction rather than being passed out on its own. Sentence frames are described as a support that lets students take part before they can build such sentences alone, which keeps the aim on moving students toward academic language rather than leaving them with the frame.
